To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the motile responses are: 1) fast (up to 10 kHz), 2) radial and transverse, 3) active, 4) electro-mechanical, 5) occur in situ, and 6) may be involved in hearing.

the outer hair cells (the sensory receptors for hearing) are able to change their length and to change their position in the cochlea, in response to electric signals, in the presence of the fluid in the organ of Cortis.

(a) the OHCs have active transverse and longitudinal motile responses; (b) the motility of the OHC is independent of the motility of other cell types in the organ of Cort; (c) the motility can be observed in the presence of metabolic inhibitors; (d) the motile responses can be recorded in situ at auditory frequencies; (e) the motility is independent of the osmotic pressure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods to investigate the motile responses of hair cells in situ.
the question of how outer hair cells are involved in the mechanical transduction process of the organ of cort.
the development of a method for the in vivo observation of motility in the organ of Cort.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present results show active motile processes of the OHC in the OC, but the exact mechanism of the motile responses and their role in the hearing process remain to be elucidated.
OHC electromotility is a transverse, fast and active process, which may contribute to cochlear amplification.
the OHCs are the most motile elements within the OC, and that they are capable of active radial and transverse movements.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the OHCs are the most motile elements in the organ of Cort.
the motile responses of the OHC are a result of a combination of the active transverse and longitudinal movements.
we have been successful in demonstrating that the OHCs are motile in situ and that their motility may play a role in the cochlear amplifier.
The main takeaway from our work is that
OHC electromotility can occur in situ in an intact cochlea.
we can now study the electromotility of OHCs within their native environment.
the outer hair cell (OHC) is not only a transducer but is also an active mechanical component of the organ of corty (OC).
